newsitem.title: PERU: Peru hostages begin Easter weekend awaiting news.
newsitem.headline: Peru hostages begin Easter weekend awaiting news.

text.p: Hostages held captive by Peru's Tupac Amaru rebels spent the Good Friday holiday eating traditional fish meals and listening to local radio for news of their fate and messages from their families.
Friday marked the 101st day of captivity for the 72 male hostages in the besieged Japanese ambassador's residence, where they were captured by the Marxist rebel group during a pre-Christmas party.
After a week that saw growing hopes for a solution to the crisis, there was a lull in expectations on Friday as Peruvians began their long Easter holiday weekend.
Government offices were closed and Roman Catholic churches held Good Friday masses including prayers for the captives.
At the neighbouring port Callao, thousands of Peruvians took part in a Via Crucis (Way of the Cross) procession in honour of the captives.
"Brothers of the MRTA," Callao's Bishop, Monsignor Miguel Irizar told the rebels referring to their group by its acronym, "In the name of God -- when are you going to free our brothers the hostages?"
"Let it be soon, do not prolongue their long Via Crucis. We ask you this on this Good Friday night."
At the residence, the Red Cross delivered fish lunches for the hostages and rebels alike and prepared for a special mass and distribution of chocolate Easter eggs on Sunday.

In contrast with the optimism earlier this week in Lima, Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said on Friday he did not foresee dramatic progress soon in talks between the government and the MRTA. "I can't say with confidence that there will be significant progress," he told reporters in Tokyo. "I am not optimistic," he added without elaborating.

The two sides have not met directly since March 12, but are believed to be nearing agreement on some points of a proposal to end the crisis put forward by a three-man guarantors commission overseeing negotiations.
Face-to-face talks between government negotiator Domingo Palermo and MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa are expected to resume on Monday or Tuesday.

Two of the guarantors -- Red Cross representative Michel Minnig and Canadian ambassador Anthony Vincent -- entered the residence in the afternoon to continue talks with the MRTA leaders. They made no comment as they left the compound.
Diplomatic sources say the hostage-takers have provisionally agreed to take asylum in Cuba, but there is still no agreement over their principal demand for the release of jailed comrades.
Media and diplomatic circles have been awash with speculation of a possible ransom payment to the MRTA and the release of some, lower-ranking prisoners to partially meet their demand.

President Alberto Fujimori said on Thursday a peaceful solution was in sight but he warned that obstacles remain. The MRTA also confirmed the two sides had moved closer but called news reports of an imminent deal "simple speculation," adding that major issues remained to be resolved.

An opinion poll showed growing discontent with the way Fujimori was handling the crisis. Although he enjoyed an early surge in popularity, the trend soon changed. The latest poll, taken last week, found approval for his handling of the longest hostage siege in Latin America's history shrinking 6.5 percentage points to 56.5 percent.

The survey by pollster Imasen, published on Friday in the daily Gestion, said 32.7 percent feel the government caused peace talks to stall during March while 24.9 percent say the MRTA is at fault and 41.6 percent blame both sides.
Relatives of the captives sought to cheer them up on Friday with songs and messages broadcast on local radio -- the hostages' only source of news from outside.

"With great affection Nandito, we hope that in this Holy Week the Lord hears our prayers so that this moment passes soon," said one relative, who, like others, used a nickname so as not to identify the hostage.
"I know that you have great strength," the message continued. "This Good Friday all our children are here. I love you. Take care of yourself. Goodbye my dear."
